newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore trader sparks huge West-East diesel flow.
newsitem.headline: Singapore trader sparks huge West-East diesel flow.

text.p: An independent Singapore-based trader has triggered what may be the largest ever flow of diesel into Asia from the West after buying huge volumes in the local market, traders said on Wednesday.
The trader -- Hin Leong Trading -- bought as much as one million tonnes in March, said traders who have tracked the deals.
The volume exceeds the average 600,000 tonnes that China, the largest diesel importer in Asia, normally takes each month.
During the buying spree, Singapore diesel prices rose 12 percent, or $3.00 per barrel, helping refiners to some of their strongest profit margins in more than a year.
At their height Singapore prices were pushed more than $4.50 per barrel above European levels and sparked a flurry of sales to Asia by European refineries.

Industry sources said they estimated that 1.0-1.6 million tonnes of diesel will be shipped to Asia and the Indian sub-continent from the Mediterranean, the Black Sea, the Baltic, North West Europe and the Middle East.
The cargoes are due to arrive from mid-April to early May, at which time the sources said prices could fall sharply unless the trader remains a heavy buyer.
The rise in diesel prices, and a simultaneous fall in crude prices, meant Singapore refiners enjoyed their best profits in more than a year.
"They have supported margins very well for Singapore refiners," one refining source said.
Singapore refining margins, based on Dubai crude oil, could average almost $2.00 per barrel on basic refining, a stark contrast to the 60-cent losses recorded in January.
But the aggressive buying by Hin Leong has raised many questions among traders. They wonder where will all the oil go and what has been the company's strategy.
Hin Leong said it had already found customers for a great percentage of the cargoes, but declined to elaborate.

The family-run business has grown over the past decade from a bunker supplier to a major independent trader, supported by sister company Ocean Tankers, which owns a fleet of about 90 tankers totalling around 2.5 million deadweight tonnes, traders said.

Some industry sources suggested that a few months ago Hin Leong sealed sales contracts with Chinese buyers on a floating price basis. Hin Leong then could have possibly hedged the sales on behalf of the buyers in the local swaps market, the sources said.
This ensured the Chinese buyers would not be disadvantaged by a rise in spot prices when the heavy physical purchases were made.

At the same time, sources said Hin Leong could have also bought March swaps on their own account, thus reaping huge profits because of the rise in the past two months of the March diesel market of more than $2.00 per barrel.
Some traders said Hin Leong only acted as a middleman for Chinese buyers. Others argued that Hin Leong has a history of large purchases of oil products on its own account.

A third theory is that Hin Leong had bought up to five million barrels of March and April swaps and at the same time sold a similar amount of May swaps and will use the physical barrels it has acquired to sell the May market down.
However, some traders said Hin Leong has placed the cargoes in its niche markets, including China, Indonesia and Vietnam.

While the industry is scratching its collective head trying to figure out how Hin Leong has managed to buy such huge volumes, most observers said the company would reap a handsome dividend from its more than U.S.$200 million foray in the local diesel market.
